lesson.title: From Single Digits to Bytes
lesson.summary: This section explains how individual bits combine into bytes, and why grouping eight bits together lets a computer represent far more than just two values.
lesson.body:
You already know that a binary number is built from digits that can only be 0 or 1. When you isolate just one of those digits and think of it as a piece of information rather than part of a larger number, you're looking at a bit ,  the smallest unit a computer can store or manipulate. A single bit can only be in one of two states, so on its own it can represent exactly two possibilities: on or off, true or false, yes or no.

The real power shows up when you start combining bits. With one bit you get 2 possible patterns. Add a second bit, and now each of those two patterns can be paired with either a 0 or a 1 in the new position, giving you 2 × 2 = 4 total combinations: 00, 01, 10, and 11. Every additional bit doubles the number of distinct patterns available, because each new bit multiplies the possibilities by 2. In general, a group of n bits can represent 2^n different values. This is the same exponential growth you saw when converting binary numbers to decimal ,  it's not a coincidence, since a group of bits is really just a binary number.

A byte is simply a fixed group of 8 bits, treated as a single unit. Using the doubling rule, 8 bits give you 2^8 = 256 distinct patterns, ranging from 00000000 up to 11111111. That's why a single byte is the standard building block computers use to represent one small piece of data, like a number from 0 to 255, or one character of text. For example, the ASCII scheme for encoding text characters only needs 128 distinct codes to cover uppercase and lowercase letters, digits, punctuation, and control characters ,  and 128 fits comfortably within the 256 patterns a single byte can produce, with room left over that later encoding systems used for additional symbols.

It helps to see why bits alone are too limited for most real tasks. If you tried to represent every letter of the alphabet using only 4 bits, you'd max out at 2^4 = 16 possible patterns ,  not even enough for 26 letters, let alone digits and punctuation. Grouping bits into a byte solves that problem cheaply: instead of needing 26 separate wires or storage cells for 26 letters, you need only 8 bits arranged in different patterns, and 256 possible arrangements is more than enough.

Keep this doubling relationship in mind, because it's the mechanism behind almost everything a computer stores or transmits. Whether you're looking at how much memory a variable takes up, how large a file is, or how many colors a pixel can display, the underlying question is always the same: how many bits are grouped together, and therefore how many distinct patterns ,  how much distinct information ,  that group can hold.
